..
KEY MESSAGE 1...

A mid-level short-wave in the northwest flow aloft over the
Northeast will bring isolated to scattered showers and
thunderstorms this afternoon. Isolated to scattered showers have
already begun to increase across the region by 18Z. The 500 hPa
temp on the 12Z KALY sounding was -11C. Mid-level lapse rates 
remain weak at less than 6C/km. The surface dewpoints are in the
50s to lower 60s with spotty mid 60s closer to the mid Hudson 
Valley in the NYS mesonet. Low-level lapse rates are steep in 
the 8-9C/km range. The latest SPC RAP Meso-analysis indicates 
MLCAPE mainly 250 J/kg or less, and we may see an increase to 
250-500 J/kg. The SBCAPE values are generally 500 J/kg or less. 
Some of the CAMs show an increase to 500-100 J/kg of SBCAPE, but
based on the present dewpoints instability is limited. However,
the 0-6 km bulk shear continues to 50-60 KT with strongest 
winds of 50-66 KT close to 500 hPa. Some low-topped 
thunderstorms are possible with gusty winds and small hail. We 
can not rule out an isolated severe storm with damaging winds, 
but the limited instability should inhibit updrafts from 
getting tall enough for a widespread severe threat. SPC placed 
the entire area in a Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 5) for an 
isolated severe threat this afternoon. PWATs are 1-1.25" and the
strong flow aloft should limit any hydro threat.

The showers and thunderstorms should diminish quickly in
the late afternoon/early evening with the short-wave passage and
the loss of the diurnal heating. Patchy fog will likely form in
the major valleys with clearing skies and recent wet ground in
spots with light to calm winds with the ridge moving in from 
southeast Canada. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...

High pressure will build in from southeast Ontario and southwest
Quebec for Saturday. After morning radiational fog burns off,
expect temps to rise from the 40s and mid 50s. Low temp readings
around 40F are possible in the southwest Adirondacks Saturday
morning. Expect mostly sunny conditons and dry weather during
the day due to the strong subsidence from the surface high. Max
temps will run slightly cooler than normal for mid-August with 
highs in the upper 70s to around 80F in the valleys and mid 60s 
to mid 70s over the hills and mtns. It will be very comfortable 
and the dry and less humid air mass with dewpoints in the mid 
40s to 50s. The surface anticyclone will move east of the region
to near southeast New England by Sunday morning. Another cool 
morning is expected with lows in the mid 40s to mid 50s again 
with some mid and high clouds increasing from the south and west
ahead of a warm front and low pressure system approaching from 
the Great Lakes Region. Some localized patchy to areas of fog 
will be possible near the CT River Valley near southeast VT and 
also the Lake George/Glens Falls area. 

The 2nd half of the weekend begins dry, but heights begin to
fall with the mid-level flow becoming nearly zonal. The low to 
mid level warm advection increases ahead of the warm front for 
showers to increase west of the Hudson River Valley/I-87 
corridor in the late morning into the early afternoon, and then 
increasing to likely to categorical PoPs (55-80%) by the late 
afternoon to early evening, as the low pressure system and mid 
and upper level short-wave approaches. 

PWATS rise above normal and the low-level moisture increases. 
Some elevated instability will in place for a slight chance of 
thunderstorms Sun pm into Sun night. The latest 24-hr NBM 
probabilities for >1" of rainfall for the period ending 8 
am/Monday are 25-60%. The 2" probabilities are generally under 
20% for the same time period. A secondary low or weak wave may 
form along the front continuing the rain well into Monday 
morning for locations south and east of Albany. However, the 
system looks progressive on the ensembles and deterministic 
guidance with 0.50-1.00" of rainfall with some 1-2" amounts 
along the southwest slopes of the Adirondacks, eastern 
Catskills, and possibly portions of western New England. WPC has
kept a Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 4) across most of the region 
for an isolated flash flood threat, though they did place the 
southern extreme of the forecast area in a Slight Risk (Level 2 
of 4) which is near the I-84 corridor, where soils are 
wetter/more saturated recently. We will continue to monitor this
event, as it appears ponding of water on roadways and poor 
drainage flooding of low-lying or urban areas would be the main 
issues, unless high rainfall rates are achieved. Drier weather 
returns Monday afternoon through Tuesday with seasonable temps, 
before another system brings some showers and thunderstorms late
Wed into Thu.
